newsitem.title: UK: Ukraine at odds over Chernobyl but closure still on.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine at odds over Chernobyl but closure still on.

text.p: Ukraine said on Sunday that it was meeting its obligations under an agreement to close the Chernobyl nuclear power station but disagreed with the recent findings of an international panel of experts.

"If conditions change there will be a special government meeting to consider possible action, but in the meantime we are following a course implementing the decisions of the memorandum," Environment Minister Yuri Kostenko told reporters.

He was referring to a December 1995 memorandum between the Ukrainian government and the Group of Seven leading industrialised nations calling for closure of Chernobyl by 2000 and a package of financial assistance worth $2.3 billion. "For more than a year Ukraine has been following all of its obligations," Kostenko said in reference to the closure of one of the four units of Chernobyl at the end of 1996 and energy sector reforms.
Chernobyl was the site of the world's worst nuclear accident in April 1986 when a fire and explosion sent clouds of radioactive particles over much of Europe and beyond.

Kostenko, speaking on the fringes of the annual meeting of the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), said Kiev disagreed with the findings of an international panel of experts chaired by Professor John Surrey.
The panel, whose report was issued in February, concluded that plans to complete construction of two other nuclear reactors in Ukraine, Khmelnitsky 2 and Rovno 4 (K2/R4), were uneconomic.
"The biggest mistake of the Surrey panel is that decommissioning of Chernobyl does not necessitate compensatory energy capacity because existing capacity is sufficient," Kostenko said.

The panel said electricity demand had fallen so sharply due to economic decline that a present surplus could last until 2010. It added that completing the K2/R4 reactors would not be the best use of $1 billion or more of funds earmarked by the EBRD and European Union.
Kostenko said there was concern over the state of 200 tonnes or so of nuclear fuel trapped under the "sarcophagus" shield of reinforced concrete around the stricken reactor.
Proposals to build a new improved protective shield had been rejected, he added. "A joint study is now being carried out on extracting the fuel from the reactor," he said.
Ukrainian National Security Council department chief Yevhen Bersheda said completion of K2/R4 was part of the overall problem of ensuring Ukraine's energy supplies.
"If completion of K2/R4 is not achieved we will be faced with a threat to the economic stability of Ukraine," he said.
Ron Freeman, first vice-president of the EBRD, told a news conference that there were doubts about financing work on the two plants.
"If the payments are not coming in, the debt service on the money that we would lend to build these two plants will not be amortised. We don't want that to happen," he said.

"We're struggling with this one to make sure it's a good deal," he added. "In banking terms it probably should not be financed 100 percent with debt. It probably needs equity or the equivalent of equity, which raises the question of privatisation."
